unit.title: Systems and Simultaneous Constraints
unit.act: Act V - Satisfying several conditions at once
unit.role: Extend linear reasoning to multiple equations, variables, and feasible regions.
unit.governingQuestion: Which values satisfy several requirements simultaneously?
unit.storyArc: Intersections represent simultaneous truth. Graphing estimates solutions, substitution replaces equals by equals, elimination combines equations to remove a variable, and applications reveal when two variables are the natural model.
outcomes: Interpret a system solution as satisfying every constraint.
Solve systems graphically, by substitution, and by elimination.
Classify one, zero, or infinitely many solutions.
Model totals, mixtures, rates, and break-even situations.
Graph systems of inequalities and interpret feasible regions.
unit.investigation: Design a production or allocation plan subject to budget, time, and minimum-output constraints.
unit.mastery: Mixed systems require method selection and interpretation of the ordered-pair solution.

lessons.outcome: Understand a solution as an ordered pair satisfying every equation or constraint.

opening.prompt: Test a candidate plan against two requirements.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make systems as simultaneous conditions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for systems as simultaneous conditions.
exposition: Understand a solution as an ordered pair satisfying every equation or constraint. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In systems as simultaneous conditions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Overlapping constraint cards. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Ordered pair tested in both equations. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.

exposition: Combine scaled equations to remove a variable while preserving the common solution. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. lessons.title: Systems of inequalities
lessons.outcome: Find regions satisfying multiple linear bounds and distinguish included boundaries.

opening.prompt: Locate feasible production or scheduling choices.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make systems of inequalities necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for systems of inequalities.
exposition: Find regions satisfying multiple linear bounds and distinguish included boundaries. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In systems of inequalities, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Layered half-planes. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Boundary inclusion. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
